searchText: This isn't a reasonable backstop when you are trying to create a credibly neutral trusted setup ceremony. "Don't worry, we trusted the trusted party at the time the trusted setup was run" isn't a compelling story to future users of the platform. In fact, I would argue that if pretty much anyone claims the sequencer refused to accept their commitment , we should assume the trusted setup is compromised. Of course, this is extremely susceptible to trolling, so really there should be a mechanism for proving that the sequencer is rejecting your commitments such as by sharing your commitment with others so *they* can submit it and witness the censorship themselves. Ideally, this would be fully automated with a gossip network, so if the sequencer says your commitment was invalid, you would then gossip it out to the network and everyone who received it would check it for validity and then attempt to submit themselves. If they also witnessed censorship, they would propagate the commitment to their peers and flag the sequencer as corrupt from their point of view. This would allow us to have pretty high confidence that if the sequencer is censoring someone's commitment, then everyone running a client would be personally witness the censorship, rather than a single person who may be crying wolf. **TL;DR**: "Don't worry, the sequencer can be trusted to not lie." is **not** an acceptable component to a trusted setup ceremony. <kevaundray> > <kevaundray> What if I submit an invalid contribution to the sequencer, then submit a valid contribution to the rest of the network? Since contributions are linked, if the sequencer says Alice's contribution is invalid, they will immediately start looking for the next contributor, whose contribution would invalidate Alice's, so in that case, the sequencer would need to wait a while after each failed contribution for dispute resolution. A sequencer censoring Alice's contribution and not Bob's does not make Bob's contribution invalid, so its possible to have a post ceremony where everyone who has been blacklisted is given a chance to contirbute via gated access to the ceremony (re @kzg_ceremony_bot: <Micah> Ideally, this would be fully automated with a gossip network, so if the sequencer says your commitment was invalid, you would then gossip it out to the network and everyone who received it would check it for validity and then attempt to submit themselves. This means the worst damage a troll can do is timeout their turn (is 15 seconds enough?), and the sequencer cannot maliciously skip/ignore anyone without a significant portion of the gossip network becoming aware of it. An honest participant will attempt to submit at the beginning of their turn. If everything goes smoothly they'll commit quickly and be accepted quickly. If the participant is a troll they will do nothing for all 3 minutes. If the sequencer is malicious, the participant will submit at the start of the 3 minutes, get ignored by the sequencer (or receive a rejection) and they'll then gossip to their peers. The peers will then submit on behalf of the censored user and also witness the censorship. This repeats until either the 3 minutes are up or the sequencer accepts. If a peer witnesses censorship in this way, they would start sounding alarm bells and potentially stop following the sequencer. If half of the gossip network has personally witnessed the censorship (because they submitted on behalf of the censored participant and the slot timed out without acceptance) then we have a strong signal that the sequencer was corrupt/censoring. We don't need 100% of the network to witness the censorship, just enough that we can be confident that it wasn't just some troll *claiming* to be censored. <kevaundray> > <kevaundray> I think a gossip network adds undue complexity here, having the sequencer save signed contributions which have been rejected in some public place sounds reasonable to counteract trolls. We need some mechanism for disambiguating these two scenarios. It doesn't have to be perfect (we don't need on-chain consensus for which happened, but we need better than two actors asserting mutually exclusive statements. The participants who witnessed censorship would quit the ceremony, believing it to be corrupt. Having that be automatic makes this a very strong credible threat to the sequencer, because their whole ceremony will likely get laughed at if they censor someone. excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Having a large number of participants while also having some censored participants makes the ceremony only valid to the large set of participants and their close connections in their trust network.  Having no censored participants extends the credibility *significantly*, because you can make the claim that anyone who *could* and wanted to participate did, and you only need one honest member of that set.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: When the set of participants is limited to only non-censored participants, while the set of potential participants included more people you no longer get to claim that anyone who could participate did.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: An adversary in the future will make the claim that, "they just censored everyone not in their cartel" and they'll point to the censored participants as "proof".

excerpts.content: If the timeout is 3 minutes, and generating the contribution takes 30 seconds, that still leaves 2.5 minutes to get your contribution on-chain (assuming you publish on-chain immediately).  If I start generating my contribution right at the start of my turn, then wait 1 minute for a receipt from the sequencer, that still leaves 1.5 minutes for my contribution to mine.  With a priority fee of 2 and sufficient base fee, that should be nearly guaranteed.  The primary concern here I think would be making sure the user has everything ready *prior* to their contribution, so when their turn shows up the whole thing can proceed automatically.

excerpts.author: carlbeek
excerpts.content: what exactly are you putting on chain here?

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Your contribution, to prove that your contribution was made available prior to the end of your slot.

excerpts.author: carlbeek
excerpts.content: unless it is the full contribution you have a data availiblilty problem

excerpts.author: carlbeek
excerpts.content: but 1 contribution is 50M gas

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: It can be in calldata.  The only purpose here is to give users a fallback *in case* they are censored, such that they can prove to the world they were censored after the fact.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: In just calldata bytes?

excerpts.author: carlbeek
excerpts.content: yes

excerpts.author: carlbeek
excerpts.content: just call data

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Bleh, well that definitely ruins that plan!

excerpts.author: kevaundray
excerpts.content: The 3 minute timeout was originally meant for those in countries with not as good CPU power or bandwidth. No benchmarks have been done on how long it takes for them to download the data etc

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: I'm open to other ideas on how we can guarantee that someone who *claims* to have been censored during the ceremony can get included in some follow-up special case ceremony.

excerpts.author: carlbeek
excerpts.content: we could probably come up with a very complicated scheme for doing so, but ultimately it is just going to be a modified blockchain.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Like maybe people can become sequencers themselves in a period after the ceremony, and we chain them end on end until no more people want to be a sequencer (with on-chain registrations and perhaps a bond or fee).

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: We already have a blockchain, it feels like we should be able to leverage that.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: We just need something that allows us to credibly say that anyone who *claims* to have been censored had a reasonable opportunity to rectify the situation after the main ceremony.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: My *guess* is that if we have a sufficiently credible mechanism, no one will claim to be censored.  🙂

excerpts.author: carlbeek
excerpts.content: but how do we hold people accountable against their bond?

excerpts.author: carlbeek
excerpts.content: we need consensus over their behaviour

excerpts.author: carlbeek
excerpts.content: in an automated fashion

excerpts.author: carlbeek
excerpts.content: some kind of state machine

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Is there any kind of proof of sequencer activity that can be provided on-chain?

excerpts.author: carlbeek
excerpts.content: not one that can verifiably solve data availability and timing problems

excerpts.author: kevaundray
excerpts.content:
I think its possible to just re-run the ceremony for those who claim foul-play with gated access (?)

They should have a signed token showing that they signed up and then we can check that they did not contribute at the end of the ceremony. If not, then give them a token to contribute in this special censorship edition of the ceremony.

excerpts.author: kevaundray
excerpts.content: There is the downside that someone could sign up and then just come back for this gated access version

excerpts.author: carlbeek
excerpts.content: yeah and now they can claim that they were censored and we lend them legitimacy by giving them a censorship participation key

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content:
The problem I'm trying to solve:
Vitalik claims on Twitter that his contribution wasn't accepted, and the sequencer claims that Vitalik never submitted a contribution.  Vitalik and the sequencer can't come to terms with each other off-line, so we need a way to resolve this in a way that proves to the public (in the future) whether the sequencer was censoring or Vitalik was lying.  Without this, the ceremony won't be accepted by most of the internet.  (replace Vitalik with some well known anti-Ethereum maximalist if that helps paint the picture).

excerpts.author: carlbeek
excerpts.content: plus who would run the sequencer then? same problem?

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Can a person commit the output of sequencing on-chain?

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: And can you commit an intermediate output on chain and then build off of that?

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: I'm guessing not in a way that is verifiable and/or doesn't have data availability problems?

excerpts.author: carlbeek
excerpts.content: Yup, pretty much

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: I'm assuming that 50M gas contribution can't be compressed in any meaningful way?

excerpts.author: carlbeek
excerpts.content: nope, by construction as close to random as we can get it

excerpts.author: carlbeek
excerpts.content: fundamentally i think the solution you are looking for is either running the sequencer as a state machine on a dedicated blockchain or some kind of (YOSO) MPC.

excerpts.author: kevaundray
excerpts.content:
What solution is there to those that claim they have been censored except for allowing them to contribute again?

We can investigate why they were censored and run the same sequencer again, since this is not a part of the protocol

------

If Vitalik is getting censored, then he can use an anonymous Eth address and hide his IP. If he is still being censored, then the sequencer is indiscriminately censoring contributors, which is easy to spot

excerpts.author: carlbeek
excerpts.content: the the is the sequencer is not actually going to censor anyone. so anyone who is claiming so is just lying so we'd need to prove that.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: You either need to give them the ability to provably contribute, or you need to give them the ability to show the censorship to many others in an easy/automated way.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Maybe if someone claims to be censored they can be given an opportunity after the main ceremony to post their contribution on IPFS and publish the hash on-chain, and then for the next `n` time anyone can check to see if the file is available on IPFS at that hash, and if it is they can try to contribute on behalf of the user.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Taken to the extreme, a claimant could have like a week long window where anyone could "audit" their claim.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Then we can build up a sufficiently large community of auditors who either validate the claim of censorship or debunk it.

excerpts.author: carlbeek
excerpts.content: but then we have to let everyone get a 1 week contribution slot

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: So now it isn't just the sequencer saying "I never saw it", but instead dozens or hundreds of well known individuals saying "I never saw it".

excerpts.author: carlbeek

excerpts.author: kevaundray
